A* es, probablemente, el algoritmo de in: A* is probably the artificial intelligence algorithm that runs most times a day in the world. It is inside any map navigator —with heuristics far finer than the block distance—, in the movement of the characters of almost every video game, in the planning of delivery routes and in warehouse robots. And it learns nothing: it works everything out afresh each time.

Con el mejor orden posible de las ramas,: With the best possible order of the branches, pruning reduces the number of leaves from $b^d$ to approximately $b^{d/2}$. That doubles the depth that can be looked at in the same time, and in chess the difference between looking six moves ahead and twelve is the difference between an amateur and a champion. That is why programs put so much effort into trying the moves that look good first: not to get it right, but to be able to prune sooner.

Conviene saber que durante cuarenta años: It is worth knowing that for forty years the artificial intelligence that worked learned absolutely nothing. Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997 without having learned a single thing from any game: it looked at two hundred million positions per second and chose. It is still like that in your GPS, in parcel delivery and in a hospital's timetables. Searching well is an alternative to learning, and it is also what a modern model ends up using as a crutch.

It reads: “f of n is g of n plus h of n”.

$g(n)$ is the real cost from the origin to $n$, which is already known. $h(n)$ is the heuristic: an estimate of what is left from $n$ to the destination, invented by whoever programs it. And $f(n)$ is the estimate of the total cost of the path going through there. The candidate with the smallest $f$ is always explored.

With $h = 0$ there is no hint and A* becomes exactly Dijkstra.

It reads: “the number of leaves is approximately b to the d”. The $b$ is the branching factor, how many moves there are on average at each turn, and the $d$ is the depth, how many turns are looked at ahead.

It is an [[fn-exp-log|exponential]], and that is why the problem is not one of faster computers. In noughts and crosses $b \approx 4$ and the whole tree has about 550,000 positions: it fits. In chess $b \approx 35$ and a game lasts about 80 turns, so the complete tree has of the order of $35^{80}$ leaves, more than there are atoms in the observable universe. It does not fit, and it never will.
Se leen <em>«alfa»</em> y <em>«beta»</em:
They read “alpha” and “beta”.

They are passed down while the tree is traversed. As soon as at some node $\alpha \ge \beta$, whatever is left to look at there cannot change the root's decision, and it is cut. It is a provably harmless cut: the value that comes out at the end is exactly the same as without pruning.
Si $h$ estima 10 donde de verdad faltan: If $h$ estimates 10 where 6 are really left, A* can accept a worse path. Admissibility is not a technical detail: it is what guarantees that the answer is the optimal one.
Si el árbol cabe, el juego está resuelto: If the tree fits, the game is solved, and you already saw the rule for solving it in [[av-juegos|game theory]]. The leaves are evaluated —I win, I lose, a draw— and the values rise towards the root alternating: on my turn I keep the maximum, because I choose; on the opponent's turn, the minimum, because they choose and you have to assume they play well.

Noughts and crosses is solved, and its value is the draw. Draughts was solved too, in 2007, after eighteen years of computation: also a draw. Chess and go will never be solved this way, and that is why something else had to be invented.
